topic: 阿波罗：人类离开地球的四年（1968 Apollo 8 — 1972 Apollo 17）

facts.claim: Apollo 8 launched on December 21, 1968 at 12:51:00 UTC (7:51 a.m. EST).
The Apollo 8 crew was Commander Frank F. Borman II, Command Module Pilot James A. Lovell Jr., and Lunar Module Pilot William A. Anders.
Apollo 8 completed ten orbits of the Moon over about twenty hours — the first time humans reached and orbited another world.
On December 24, 1968, during their ninth lunar orbit, the Apollo 8 crew read the first ten verses of the Book of Genesis in a live television broadcast.
An estimated quarter of the people alive at the time saw or heard the Apollo 8 Christmas Eve transmission, live or delayed.

The Apollo 8 Christmas Eve broadcast drew an audience of roughly one billion people across five continents — about one in four people on the planet — and was the most-watched television program to that date.
facts.source_title: Remembering the Apollo 8 Christmas Eve Broadcast — HISTORY

facts.claim: NASA notes the Apollo 8 crew planned the Christmas Eve reading as something appropriate for a global, religiously diverse audience, and that Earthrise 'would give humankind a new perspective on their home planet'.
facts.source_title: Apollo 8: Christmas at the Moon — NASA

facts.claim: The color Earthrise photograph is NASA frame AS08-14-2383, taken by William Anders on December 24, 1968 at 16:39:39.3 UTC.
Earthrise was shot on a highly modified electric-drive Hasselblad 500 EL with a 250 mm lens on custom Kodak Ektachrome film; Anders took a black-and-white frame first, then called for color film.
Apollo 8 splashed down on December 27, 1968 at 15:51:42 UTC in the North Pacific Ocean southwest of Hawaii.
The Apollo 8 mission lasted 6 days, 3 hours, 0 minutes, 42 seconds.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969 at 13:32:00 UTC (9:32 a.m. EDT) from Kennedy Space Center.
The Apollo 11 crew was Commander Neil Armstrong, Command Module Pilot Michael Collins, and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin 'Buzz' Aldrin Jr.
The Apollo 11 lunar module was named Eagle and the command and service module was named Columbia.
Eagle landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969 at 20:17:40 UTC.

The Apollo 11 landing site was named Tranquility Base, in Mare Tranquillitatis (the Sea of Tranquility); Armstrong changed the call sign from 'Eagle' to 'Tranquility Base' to signal the landing had succeeded.
Neil Armstrong set his left boot on the lunar surface at 02:56:15 UTC on July 21, 1969 — 10:56 p.m. EDT on July 20 in the United States — about six hours after landing.

Armstrong's words on stepping onto the Moon were 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind'; the recording does not clearly carry the indefinite article, which Armstrong later conceded he must have dropped.
The single Apollo 11 surface EVA lasted 2 hours, 31 minutes, 40 seconds.
Apollo 11 returned 21.5 kg (47.5 lb) of lunar samples.
Apollo 11 splashed down on July 24, 1969.
Armstrong's moonwalk was broadcast live to an estimated 600 million viewers.
An alternative widely cited figure puts the worldwide audience for Armstrong's first steps at an estimated 650 million viewers.
facts.source_title: From the Moon to your living room: the Apollo 11 broadcast — National Science and Media Museum

facts.claim: Apollo 12 launched on November 14, 1969 at 16:22:00 UTC (11:22 a.m. EST) from Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A.
The Apollo 12 crew was Commander Charles 'Pete' Conrad Jr., Command Module Pilot Richard F. Gordon Jr., and Lunar Module Pilot Alan L. Bean — all three US Navy officers.
The Apollo 12 launch vehicle was struck twice by lightning shortly after liftoff; Mission Control's corrective action recovered the telemetry and the mission continued.
Apollo 12 landed on November 19, 1969 just 535 feet (163 m) from the Surveyor 3 probe, demonstrating pinpoint landing capability.
The Apollo 12 crew removed and returned several pieces of Surveyor 3, including its television camera, after the probe had spent two and a half years on the Moon.
Apollo 12 returned 73.75 pounds (33.45 kg) of lunar samples and splashed down on November 24, 1969 at 20:58 UTC in the South Pacific Ocean.
Apollo 13 launched on April 11, 1970 at 19:13:00 UTC (2:13 p.m. EST).
The Apollo 13 crew that flew was Commander James A. Lovell Jr., Command Module Pilot John L. 'Jack' Swigert Jr., and Lunar Module Pilot Fred W. Haise Jr.

Ken Mattingly was replaced as Apollo 13 Command Module Pilot by Jack Swigert two days before launch: backup crew member Charles Duke had contracted rubella, and Mattingly was the only one of the five astronauts training together who lacked immunity.
The Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure occurred at mission elapsed time 55:54:53 — 03:08 UTC on April 14, 1970 (10:08 p.m. EST, April 13).

The cause of the Apollo 13 accident was damaged Teflon insulation on the stirring-fan wiring inside oxygen tank 2, which short-circuited and ignited when Swigert switched the fans on at Mission Control's request.

Twenty-six seconds after the bang, Swigert transmitted 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here'; at 55:55:42 Lovell said 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus undervolt.' The film line 'Houston, we have a problem' is not the flown wording.
Apollo 13 abandoned the landing, used the lunar module Aquarius as a lifeboat, and looped around the Moon on a free-return trajectory instead of turning back directly.
At pericynthion on April 14, 1970 the Apollo 13 crew reached 400,171 kilometers (248,655 mi) from Earth — the record for the farthest humans have travelled from Earth.

The Apollo 13 distance record stood for over 55 years and was broken on April 6, 2026, when the Artemis II crew (Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen) reached a maximum 252,756 miles from Earth, about 4,100 miles beyond Apollo 13's mark.
facts.source_title: NASA's Artemis II Astronauts Break Apollo's Distance Record — Scientific American

facts.claim: Apollo 13 splashed down safely in the South Pacific Ocean on April 17, 1970 after a mission of 5 days, 22 hours, 54 minutes, 41 seconds.

NASA frame AS13-59-8500 (also catalogued AS13-59-8500A, 17 April 1970) shows the severely damaged Apollo 13 Service Module photographed from the LM/CM after jettison; an entire SM panel was blown away by the explosion of oxygen tank 2 in Sector 4, with two of the three fuel cells visible above the damage.
facts.source_title: Astronaut Photo AS13-59-8500 — NASA JSC Earth Observation

facts.claim: NASA publishes the damaged-Service-Module frame in its own image collection as 'Damage From Apollo 13 Explosion'.
Apollo 14 launched on January 31, 1971 at 21:03:02 UTC (4:03:02 p.m. EST) after a 40-minute-2-second weather hold — the first launch delay in the Apollo program.
The Apollo 14 crew was Commander Alan B. Shepard Jr., Command Module Pilot Stuart A. Roosa, and Lunar Module Pilot Edgar D. Mitchell.

Alan Shepard was one of the Mercury Seven and the first American in space (1961); grounded by Ménière's disease, he returned to flight status after experimental surgery in 1968 and at age 47 became the oldest person to walk on the Moon.

Apollo 14 landed in the Fra Mauro formation on February 5, 1971 — the site Apollo 13 had been aiming for — returned 94.35 pounds (42.80 kg) of Moon rocks, and splashed down on February 9, 1971 in the South Pacific.
Apollo 15 launched on July 26, 1971 at 9:34 a.m. EDT.
The Apollo 15 crew was Commander David Scott, Command Module Pilot Alfred Worden, and Lunar Module Pilot James Irwin; the lunar module was Falcon and the CSM Endeavour.
Apollo 15 marked the first use of the Lunar Roving Vehicle, and landed in the Hadley–Apennine region at 26°07′56″N 3°38′02″E.
Apollo 15 drove 27.9 km (17.3 mi) on the lunar surface.
The Lunar Roving Vehicle article gives Apollo 15's rover total as 17.25 miles (27.76 km), with a longest single traverse of 7.75 miles (12.47 km).
The Lunar Roving Vehicle weighed 460 pounds (210 kg) empty and carried up to 970 pounds (440 kg) of payload; it was 10 ft (3.0 m) long with a 7.5 ft (2.3 m) wheelbase and stood 3.6 ft (1.1 m) high.
The rover was designed for a top speed of 6 mph (10 km/h); the fastest speed actually recorded was 11.2 mph (18 km/h) on Apollo 17.
The Lunar Roving Vehicle was built by Boeing with General Motors as mobility-system subcontractor, at a final cost of $38 million (about $302 million in present-day dollars per the source).
The Genesis Rock was collected at Spur crater during Apollo 15's second EVA; it is an anorthosite believed to be a piece of the Moon's early crust.

The Genesis Rock is catalogued as lunar sample 15415, a ferroan anorthosite with a mass of about 269 grams; radiometric studies indicate an age of about 4.1 billion years, likely a metamorphic reset age with the rock itself older.

At the end of the final Apollo 15 moonwalk, David Scott dropped a falcon feather and a geological hammer together on camera to demonstrate Galileo's principle that objects fall at the same rate in a gravity field regardless of mass.

Apollo 15 logged 19 hours, 7 minutes, 53 seconds of lunar surface EVA (including a 33-minute-7-second stand-up EVA), returned 77 kg (170 lb) of samples, and splashed down on August 7, 1971 at 20:45:53 UTC in the North Pacific.

Apollo 16 launched on April 16, 1972 at 17:54:00 UTC with Commander John W. Young, Command Module Pilot Thomas K. Mattingly II (the astronaut bumped from Apollo 13), and Lunar Module Pilot Charles M. Duke Jr.
Apollo 16 landed in the Descartes Highlands, chosen because some scientists expected volcanic terrain — a hypothesis the samples disproved.

Apollo 16 drove 26.7 km (16.6 mi), logged 20 hours 14 minutes 14 seconds of EVA, returned 95.71 kg (211.0 lb) of samples including Big Muley — the largest Moon rock brought back by Apollo — and splashed down on April 27, 1972.
Apollo 17 launched on December 7, 1972 at 12:33 a.m. EST from Launch Pad 39A on Saturn V SA-512 — the only night launch of the crewed Saturn V program.
The Apollo 17 crew was Commander Eugene A. Cernan, Command Module Pilot Ronald E. Evans Jr., and Lunar Module Pilot Harrison 'Jack' H. Schmitt; the lunar module was Challenger and the CSM America.
Harrison Schmitt was the only professional geologist to land on the Moon.
Apollo 17 landed in the Taurus–Littrow valley at 20.16° north, 30.77° east.
Apollo 17's three moonwalks totalled 22 hours, 3 minutes, 57 seconds (7:11:53 + 7:36:56 + 7:15:08).
NASA's mission-details page rounds Apollo 17's lunar surface EVA to 22 hours 4 minutes and gives the rover traverse as 30.5 kilometers.
Apollo 17's rover odometer total is given as approximately 35.7 km (22.2 mi) on the mission page and 22.30 miles (35.89 km) on the rover page, with the longest single traverse 12.50 miles (20.12 km).
At Shorty crater, Schmitt found orange soil made of very small beads of volcanic glass formed over 3.5 billion years ago.

The orange soil is catalogued as lunar sample 74220 (about 1,180 grams collected): orange volcanic glass beads plus black ilmenite particles, pyroclastic in origin and roughly 3.6 billion years old — the same age as the mare basalts.
facts.source_title: Lunar Sample Compendium 74220 — Lunar and Planetary Institute

facts.claim: NASA states Apollo 17 astronauts gathered 110.4 kilograms, or 243 pounds, of lunar material — the largest sample return of any Apollo mission.
Wikipedia's Apollo 17 article gives the sample return as approximately 115 kg (254 lb), a figure also used in NASA's 50th-anniversary feature.

The Blue Marble is NASA frame AS17-148-22727, taken on December 7, 1972 at 10:39 UTC (05:39 a.m. EST) about 5 hours 6 minutes after the Apollo 17 launch, from roughly 29,400 kilometers (18,300 mi) from Earth's surface.

NASA credits the Blue Marble to the Apollo 17 crew collectively; evidence and later interviews point to Harrison Schmitt as the photographer. It was shot on a 70 mm Hasselblad 500 EL with an 80 mm Zeiss Planar lens on Kodak SO-368 Ektachrome at f/2.8, 1/250 s.
NASA records that Apollo 17's third and final EVA ended at 5:40:56 a.m. on December 14, 1972, the moment Eugene Cernan left the lunar surface as the last human to stand on the Moon.

Cernan's closing words on the lunar surface, as NASA quotes them: 'as I take man's last step from the surface … — but we believe not too long into the future — I'd like to just (say) what I believe history will record. That America's challenge of today has forged man's destiny of tomorrow. And, as we leave the Moon at Taurus-Littrow, we leave as we came and, God willing, as we shall return, with peace and hope for all mankind.'
facts.source_title: 50 Years Ago: Apollo 17 Lands at Taurus-Littrow — NASA

facts.claim: Apollo 17 splashed down on December 19, 1972 in the Pacific Ocean, recovered by USS Ticonderoga, after a mission of 12 days, 13 hours, 51 minutes, 59 seconds.
Nine crewed Apollo missions flew to the Moon (Apollo 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17); six of them landed. NASA's program page lists 11 crewed missions in total and 6 lunar landing missions.
Twenty-four Apollo astronauts travelled to the Moon and twelve of them walked on its surface.
The Apollo program returned 842 pounds (382 kg) of lunar rock and soil to Earth.
The Apollo program cost $25.4 billion in 1973 dollars, equivalent to about $257 billion in 2020 dollars.
At its peak the Apollo program employed 400,000 people and required the support of over 20,000 industrial firms and universities.
The Saturn V stood 111 m (363 ft) tall with a 10 m (33 ft) core diameter.
The Saturn V first stage produced 33,000 kN (7,500,000 lbf) of thrust at sea level, and the vehicle's liftoff mass ranged from 2,822,171 to 2,965,241 kg (6,221,823 to 6,537,238 lb).

The Saturn V could place 140,000 kg (310,000 lb) into low Earth orbit and send 43,500 kg (95,900 lb) toward the Moon; thirteen were launched between 1967 and 1973, built by Boeing (S-IC), North American Aviation (S-II) and Douglas Aircraft (S-IVB).

NASA frame AS11-40-5903 shows Buzz Aldrin facing the camera on the lunar surface, with the Lunar Module, the flag and Armstrong reflected in his visor; it was taken by Neil Armstrong on 20 July 1969 at Tranquility Base with a 70 mm lunar surface camera, 60 mm lens, on Ektachrome EF SO168 color film.
facts.source_title: Astronaut Photo AS11-40-5903 — NASA JSC Earth Observation

facts.claim: NASA frame AS11-40-5878 (20 July 1969) is a close-up view of an astronaut's bootprint in the lunar soil, photographed with the 70 mm lunar surface camera during the Apollo 11 EVA.
The companion bootprint frame AS11-40-5877 shows Buzz Aldrin's bootprint together with his boot; 5877 and 5878 are the two frames of the same soil-mechanics sequence.
facts.source_title: Buzz Aldrin's bootprint on the Moon, AS11-40-5877 — Wikimedia Commons

facts.claim: The Apollo 11 image of Aldrin descending the Lunar Module ladder is NASA frame AS11-40-5868, taken by Neil Armstrong with the 70 mm lunar surface camera and 60 mm lens on Ektachrome EF SO168; the deck brief's proposed 'AS11-40-5875' is not the ladder frame.
facts.source_title: Aldrin Descends Lunar Module Ladder — NASA

facts.claim: The famous image of Harrison Schmitt beside the Station 6 boulder (Tracy's Rock, Split Rock) is NASA frame AS17-140-21496, part of a panorama sequence AS17-140-21493 to 21497 photographed by Gene Cernan on December 13, 1972 at Taurus–Littrow during EVA-3, with the Lunar Roving Vehicle parked to the right.

AS17-134-20463 is a real Apollo 17 frame (magazine 134/B covers AS17-134-20376 to 20532, EVA-1 and EVA-3 color exposures on SO-368 with a 60 mm lens), but NASA's JSC photo database returns 'Image Caption: none' for it, so it cannot be confirmed as the Schmitt-at-Tracy's-Rock image.
facts.source_title: Astronaut Photo AS17-134-20463 — NASA JSC Earth Observation

facts.claim: Apollo 17 magazine 134/B (frames AS17-134-20376 to 20532) contains the EVA-1 images of the flag, Commander Cernan and Earth, and the Station 1 panoramas.
facts.source_title: Apollo Image Atlas, 70mm Hasselblad Image Catalog, magazine 134 — Lunar and Planetary Institute

facts.claim: NASA frame AS15-88-11866 shows Lunar Module Pilot James B. Irwin giving a military salute beside the deployed U.S. flag during the Apollo 15 lunar surface EVA at the Hadley–Apennine landing site, with the LM Falcon and Hadley Delta behind him; it was taken by Commander David R. Scott.
facts.source_title: Astronaut Photo AS15-88-11866 — NASA JSC Earth Observation

facts.claim: NASA states that NASA content — images, audio, video and media files — generally is not subject to copyright in the United States; attribution to NASA is requested, and separate clearance applies to NASA logos, identifiable individuals in commercial use, and any third-party material marked as copyrighted.
facts.source_title: Images and Media — NASA Brand Center

facts.source_title: 阿波罗计划 — 维基百科

facts.source_title: 阿波罗8号 — 维基百科

facts.claim: Apollo 12 Chinese crew renderings follow the same convention: 查尔斯·'皮特'·康拉德 (Charles 'Pete' Conrad), 理查德·戈登 (Richard Gordon), 艾伦·比恩 (Alan Bean); Apollo 14: 艾伦·谢泼德 (Alan Shepard), 斯图尔特·罗萨 (Stuart Roosa), 埃德加·米切尔 (Edgar Mitchell); Apollo 16: 约翰·杨 (John Young), 托马斯·马丁利 (Thomas Mattingly), 查尔斯·杜克 (Charles Duke).
facts.source_title: 阿波罗计划 — 维基百科
